title: Honest weights (Deuteronomy 25:13–15)
hookLine: "a perfect and just weight shalt thou have"

lines: A SECOND ONE IN THE BAG.
cards: Nobody in line can see whether the brass weight on the market scale is honest. On one side, the weight; on the other, the buyer's lentils. It looks like any other weight.

The seller knows, though. And if there's a second one in his bag, slightly heavier for buying, slightly lighter for selling, he knows that too. Leviticus asked for honest weights, as this path saw in Kedoshim.
Deuteronomy goes right into the bag: "a perfect and just weight shalt thou have."

teach.b: Deuteronomy, chapter twenty-five, says it in three short lines.
Don't keep two kinds of weights in your bag, a great and a small. Don't keep two kinds of measures in your house, a great and a small. "A perfect and just weight shalt thou have."

First, the stone. The Hebrew word the verse uses for a weight is even, which also means a stone, so the verse reads: don't have a stone and a stone. It's a picture of one person holding two truths, one for each customer.
Second, the bag and the house. The verse doesn't only forbid using a false weight. It forbids owning one.
The temptation is cut off before the sale begins. Third, two words.
The weight must be shlemah, whole or perfect, and tzedek, just. Whole means nothing shaved off. Just means fair to the person on the other side.
Justice here isn't an abstract idea; it sits in a merchant's bag. Fourth, the question at the end.

teach.h: DID YOU DEAL IN GOOD FAITH?
teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, lists questions a person is asked after this life, and the first it names is: did you deal in good faith? Not, at first, how much did you study, or how often did you pray.
The verse ends with a promise: that thy days may be long upon the land.
An honest scale, in this telling, is something a whole society stands on.

how: Jewish business ethics, drawn from verses like these, is studied as part of Jewish law, and some observant merchants and professionals bring questions about pricing, measures and disclosure to their rabbis.

o: heavy stones once used to anchor a market stall
one true standard for everyone, nothing shaved off
a tax paid on goods sold at the city market

p: a stone, used as a weight
just, fair to the other side
did you deal in good faith?

s: the Torah only forbids using a false weight, not owning one
it says not to have two kinds of weights in your bag or two measures in your house.
the verse asks for a weight that is both whole and just
Deuteronomy says a perfect and just weight: nothing shaved off, and fair to the other side.
the first question the Talmud names is about prayer
in tractate Shabbat the first question named is: did you deal in good faith?

games.q: you sell grain. a slightly lighter weight sits in your bag, unused for months. what does Deuteronomy say to do?
o: keep it, as long as you never use it.
don't keep it in your bag at all.
use it only with customers who haggle.
games.why: the verse forbids having two kinds of weights in your bag, not only using them. the temptation is cut off before the sale.

practice: Let one deal from your day come to mind, however small: a price you quote, an expense you report, a used thing you're selling, the hours you log, a review you write.

Ask whether there's a second weight in your bag there: a rounding up, a detail left out, a story that sounds better than it was. If there is, set it down, and picture the whole exchange done with one honest weight.

wordCard.voice: Honest weights. In Hebrew, even shlemah va-tzedek: a whole and just stone, one weight for everyone. Today's word.
